title: Krug v. New Jersey State Parole Board
description: Whether the State Parole Board's determination to consider all relevant information about appellant Fred Krug, rather than only "new information" filed since his last parole hearing, violated the ex post facto protections of the federal and state constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: Krug argued that the Board's retroactive application of the 1997 amendment, which allowed consideration of all information, violated ex post facto laws because the 1979 Act (in effect for much of his incarceration) limited consideration to only new information, thereby increasing his punishment.
defendant_argument: The Parole Board argued that the proper baseline for ex post facto analysis is the 1948 Parole Act, which was in place when Krug committed his crimes and allowed consideration of all information, thus the 1997 amendment did not increase his punishment.
decision_outcome: The Court affirmed the Appellate Division's judgment, rejecting Krug's ex post facto challenge, finding that the retroactive application of the 1997 amendment did not create a risk of additional punishment.

title: Kratovil v. City of New Brunswick
description: Whether Daniel's Law, which prohibits the publication of certain public officials' home addresses, violates a journalist's constitutional rights to freedom of speech and press when applied to truthful, lawfully obtained information of public concern.
plaintiff_argument: Charles Kratovil argued that Daniel's Law, as applied to him, violates the New Jersey Constitution's guarantees of freedom of speech and press because he lawfully obtained truthful information (Caputo's home address) on a matter of public concern (Caputo's residency affecting his public duties) and the law is not narrowly tailored.
defendant_argument: The City of New Brunswick and Anthony A. Caputo argued that Caputo's precise home address is not a matter of public concern and that Daniel's Law serves a state interest of the highest order (protecting public officials and their families from harm) and is narrowly tailored to achieve this purpose.
decision_outcome: The Court affirmed the trial court's judgment, concluding that Daniel's Law, as applied to prevent the publication of a public official's home address, is constitutional and does not violate freedom of speech or press guarantees.

title: In re Concerning The State Grand Jury
description: Whether the trial court prematurely declined to empanel a special grand jury and suppressed a potential presentment concerning clergy abuse within the Catholic Church, which the State argued was authorized by law, but the Diocese contended was not.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued it has the right to proceed with its investigation and present evidence before a special grand jury, and that the challenge to a hypothetical presentment was premature as no grand jury had yet issued one.
defendant_argument: The Diocese of Camden argued that the anticipated presentment was not authorized by law because priests are not public officials and the Catholic Church is not a public entity, and the subject matter was not of "imminent concern" or a "public affair or condition."
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower courts' decisions, ruling that the trial court prematurely declined to empanel a special grand jury and suppressed a potential presentment, affirming the State's right to proceed with its investigation.

title: In re Tom Malinowski
description: Whether New Jersey's anti-fusion statute, N.J.S.A. 19:13-8, which prohibits a candidate from accepting more than one nomination for the same public office, violates the State Constitution's guarantees of the right to vote, free speech and political association, assembly, and equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The Moderate Party and individual voters argued that N.J.S.A. 19:13-8 violates the State Constitution by infringing on the rights to vote, free speech, political association, assembly, and equal protection, and sought to list Tom Malinowski as their nominee despite his prior Democratic Party nomination.
defendant_argument: The New Jersey Secretary of State contended that anti-fusion laws are permissible under the Federal Constitution, and the State Constitution's protections are equivalent, arguing the statute serves legitimate regulatory interests in preventing ballot manipulation, voter confusion, and maintaining political system stability.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the New Jersey Secretary of State's decision, holding that N.J.S.A. 19:13-8, the anti-fusion statute, does not violate the State Constitution.

title: Englewood Hospital & Medical Center v. State
description: Whether New Jersey's charity care program, which requires hospitals to provide care to low-income patients without full reimbursement, constitutes an unconstitutional taking of private property without just compensation, with plaintiffs arguing it is a taking and defendants arguing it is a legitimate regulation in a highly regulated industry.
plaintiff_argument: The charity care program compels hospitals to provide access to facilities, supplies, and services for charity care patients, but the subsidies do not cover the basic costs, thus violating federal and state constitutional protections against unlawful takings and infringing on their right to exclude others from their property.
defendant_argument: The charity care program is not a "per se" physical taking as it does not physically appropriate property or remove all beneficial uses, nor is it a regulatory taking under the Penn Central test, given the highly regulated nature of the hospital industry and the paramount public interest it serves.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's judgment, holding that New Jersey's charity care program does not constitute an unconstitutional "per se" physical taking or a "regulatory" taking of private property without just compensation.

title: Usachenok v. Department of the Treasury
description: Whether a state regulation requiring investigators to "request" that individuals not discuss harassment and discrimination investigations with others is an unconstitutional overbroad restraint on free speech.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Viktoriya Usachenok, argued that the regulation violates her right to free speech under the State Constitution, is unconstitutionally overbroad and vague, and operates as an unconstitutional restraint on speech.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the confidentiality request is truly a request, not a directive, and therefore neither the State nor Federal Constitution is implicated, with no adverse consequences for declining the request.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's judgment, struck down the last sentence of N.J.A.C. 4A:7-3.1(j) as unconstitutionally overbroad, and remanded the matter to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: State v. Hill
description: Whether the State's witness tampering statute, N.J.S.A. 2C:28-5(a), is unconstitutionally overbroad on its face or was unconstitutionally applied to defendant William Hill.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the witness tampering statute regulates conduct, not speech, and is not facially overbroad, serving a paramount state interest in preventing witness tampering.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the witness tampering statute is unconstitutionally overbroad because it criminalizes protected speech based on a negligence standard, violating the First Amendment.
decision_outcome: The court held that the witness tampering statute is not facially overbroad but may have been unconstitutionally applied to the defendant, vacating his witness tampering conviction and remanding for a new trial, while upholding his carjacking conviction.

title: State v. Fair
description: Whether a prosecution for terroristic threats under N.J.S.A. 2C:12-3(a) premised on a mens rea of recklessness is constitutional under the First Amendment and Article I, Paragraph 6 of the New Jersey Constitution, and whether a specific unanimity instruction is required for subsections (a) and (b).
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that N.J.S.A. 2C:12-3(a) is constitutional with a recklessness mens rea for true threats and that a specific unanimity instruction was not required for the different subsections of the statute.
defendant_argument: Calvin Fair argued that the 'reckless disregard' portion of N.J.S.A. 2C:12-3(a) is unconstitutionally overbroad, requiring a higher intent standard for his alleged political speech, and that the jury instructions and verdict sheet were flawed, necessitating a specific unanimity instruction.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, remanding the case for a new trial with instructions for a revised recklessness standard and a specific unanimity charge for the jury.

title: State v. Cohen
description: Whether the odor of marijuana in a vehicle authorizes a search of the engine compartment and trunk under the automobile exception to the warrant requirement, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Trooper Travis had probable cause to search the engine compartment and trunk based on the smell of marijuana, and urged the Court to affirm the Appellate Division's judgment.
defendant_argument: Defendant argued that the smell of marijuana alone did not provide probable cause to search the engine compartment and trunk, contending that the trial court and Appellate Division unfairly broadened prior legal holdings and that only a small amount for personal use was indicated, not a drug cache.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Appellate Division's judgment, finding that the motion to suppress the evidence seized from the engine compartment and trunk should have been granted, and remanded the case for further proceedings, allowing the defendant to withdraw his guilty plea.

title: State v. Watson
description: Whether first-time in-court identifications and investigator narration of video recordings are permissible under evidentiary rules and due process, and whether testimony about consultation with other law enforcement agencies violates the Confrontation Clause.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the in-court identification was permissible, Sergeant Vitelli's narration testimony was properly admitted under N.J.R.E. 701, and any Confrontation Clause error was harmless.
defendant_argument: Watson argued that first-time in-court identifications are inherently unreliable and unduly prejudicial, Sergeant Vitelli's narration testimony was inadmissible, and the Confrontation Clause was violated, requiring reversal.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the defendant's conviction and remanded the case for a new trial, ruling that the first-time in-court identification and certain narration testimony were improper, and the Confrontation Clause was violated.

title: Facebook, Inc. v. State
description: Whether law enforcement officials can obtain the contents of electronic communications from a Facebook account prospectively, every 15 minutes for 30 days into the future, based solely on a showing of probable cause.
plaintiff_argument: Facebook argues that neither federal nor state statutory law authorizes the use of a search warrant to compel disclosure of prospective communications, maintaining that such searches are governed by the enhanced privacy protections of wiretap acts.
defendant_argument: The State of New Jersey contends that the wiretap acts do not apply because the stored messages it seeks will not be intercepted contemporaneously, in real time, and that a Communications Data Warrant (CDW) based on probable cause is sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's judgment and quashed the parts of the Communications Data Warrants (CDWs) that directed Facebook to provide prospective electronic communications, holding that the heightened protections of New Jersey's wiretap act apply.

title: State v. Smart
description: Whether the automobile exception to the warrant requirement permitted the warrantless search of defendant Kyle Smart's vehicle, specifically whether the police actions giving rise to probable cause were "unforeseeable and spontaneous" as required under State v. Witt.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the police did not "sit" on probable cause and the circumstances leading to probable cause were "unforeseen and spontaneous," thus justifying the warrantless search under the automobile exception.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the circumstances giving rise to probable cause were not "unforeseeable or spontaneous" because the police deliberately orchestrated the investigation, including calling a canine unit, and therefore a warrant was required.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order suppressing the physical evidence seized from the defendant's vehicle, ruling that a warrant was required.

title: State v. Chambers
description: Whether a defendant in a sexual assault case can obtain pre-incident mental health records of the victim, balancing the victim's privacy and the defendant's right to a meaningful defense.
plaintiff_argument: The State (Plaintiff-Appellant) argued that mental health records are not in their possession, custody, or control, and that a heightened discovery standard should apply to protect victims from deterring reporting crimes or seeking treatment.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Defendant-Respondent) argued for access to the victim's pre-incident mental health records to present a meaningful defense, proposing a lower standard for in camera review than a "particularized need," based on a reasonable suspicion of mental illness directly related to the victim's ability to perceive, recall, or recount the event.
decision_outcome: The Court vacated the trial court's orders and remanded the matter for further proceedings, establishing a new heightened procedural and analytical framework for defendants' requests for pre-incident mental health records of sexual assault victims.

title: Moynihan v. Lynch
description: Whether N.J.S.A. 25:1-5(h)'s attorney-review requirement for palimony agreements violates the New Jersey Constitution's substantive due process guarantee, thereby rendering a written palimony agreement unenforceable without independent legal counsel.
plaintiff_argument: Moynihan argued that the written palimony agreement was valid and enforceable, and that the attorney-review requirement of N.J.S.A. 25:1-5(h) was unconstitutional, or alternatively, an oral palimony agreement existed.
defendant_argument: Lynch contended that the written agreement was unenforceable due to the lack of attorney review as required by N.J.S.A. 25:1-5(h), which he argued was constitutional, and denied the existence of an oral palimony agreement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Appellate Division in part, holding that the attorney-review requirement of N.J.S.A. 25:1-5(h) is unconstitutional, making the written palimony agreement enforceable, and affirmed that no oral palimony agreement existed.

title: Matter of Congressional Districts by New Jersey Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the New Jersey Congressional Redistricting Commission's adopted map should be vacated due to alleged arbitrary and unreasonable actions by the Chair, procedural due process violations, and a conflict of interest.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs (Republican delegation) argued that the Chair's decision to adopt the Democratic map was arbitrary, capricious, and unreasonable, violating due process rights, and that the Chair had a conflict of interest, thus the map should be vacated.
defendant_argument: The defendants (Democratic delegation) argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing, the complaint presented a non-justiciable political question, and the complaint failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted, as the map itself was not alleged to be unlawful or discriminatory.
decision_outcome: The court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the complaint with prejudice, finding the plaintiffs' allegations insufficient to support a claim for relief.

title: State v. Comer
description: Whether mandatory minimum sentences of at least 30 years without parole for juveniles, as required by N.J.S.A. 2C:11-3(b)(1), violate federal and state constitutional provisions against cruel and unusual punishment.
plaintiff_argument: The State and Attorney General argued that the homicide statute, including its mandatory minimum features, is constitutional as applied to juveniles and does not constitute cruel and unusual punishment, urging the Court to defer to the Legislature.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that mandatory sentences of at least 30 years without parole for juveniles are unconstitutional, violating federal and state prohibitions against cruel and unusual punishment, as they divest judges of discretion to consider mitigating factors related to youth and diminished moral culpability.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that while the homicide statute itself is not unconstitutional, juvenile offenders sentenced to lengthy periods of parole ineligibility must be afforded an opportunity to petition for sentence review after serving two decades in prison, consistent with state constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

title: State v. Melvin
description: Whether a trial judge can consider at sentencing a defendant's alleged conduct for crimes for which a jury returned a not guilty verdict.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that judges have broad discretion to consider all relevant evidence, including acquitted conduct, when sentencing within statutory limits, and that this does not violate constitutional mandates.
defendant_argument: Defendants argued that using acquitted conduct for sentencing violates due process and fundamental fairness, as it undermines the finality of jury verdicts and the presumption of innocence.
decision_outcome: The court held that fundamental fairness under the New Jersey Constitution prohibits trial judges from enhancing sentences based on conduct for which a jury acquitted the defendant, reversing Melvin's sentence and affirming the Appellate Division's vacating of Paden-Battle's sentence, remanding both cases for resentencing before different judges.

title: State v. McQueen
description: Whether an arrestee and the person they call have a constitutionally protectible privacy interest in a telephone conversation made from a police station line when neither party is aware the call is being recorded.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that an arrestee, and by extension the person they call, has no reasonable expectation of privacy in a police station phone call, especially given the general knowledge that police department telephones are recorded and the institutional security interests involved.
defendant_argument: Allen-Brewer argued that the warrantless recording of her conversation with McQueen violated both Federal and State Constitutions, asserting a reasonable expectation of privacy in a police station phone call, particularly without notice of recording.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's judgment, upholding the suppression of the recorded telephone conversation made from the police station, finding that an arrestee has a reasonable expectation of privacy in such calls without notice of recording.

title: State v. Carter
description: Whether N.J.S.A. 39:3-33 prohibits license plate frames that conceal or obscure any part of any marking on a license plate, including slogans, and whether an officer's reasonable mistake of law can justify a traffic stop under the New Jersey Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that N.J.S.A. 39:3-33 prohibits covering any part of any marking on a license plate, even if readable, and that an officer's objectively reasonable mistake of law should justify a stop.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that N.J.S.A. 39:3-33 should be narrowly interpreted to only prohibit covering illegible or unidentifiable markings, not cosmetic slogans, and that the 'reasonable mistake of law' doctrine should not be adopted under the New Jersey Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court held that N.J.S.A. 39:3-33 requires all license plate markings to be legible or identifiable; thus, Roman-Rosado's stop was unlawful as his slogan was recognizable, while Carter's stop was lawful as his slogan was entirely covered. The court also declined to adopt the 'reasonable mistake of law' doctrine under the New Jersey Constitution, leading to the suppression of evidence in Roman-Rosado's case.

title: State v. Andujar
description: Whether the prosecution's unilateral and selective criminal history check on a prospective juror, F.G., constituted racial discrimination that violated the defendant's right to a fair trial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that F.G.'s background and associations with criminal activity made him problematic, justifying the criminal history check and his removal for cause, and that these reasons were race-neutral.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the State's selective criminal history check on F.G., a Black male, was racially discriminatory, violated his right to a fair trial by an impartial jury, and that prosecutors should not unilaterally conduct such checks.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the defendant's conviction and remanded the case for a new trial, finding that the jury selection process was tainted by implicit or unconscious racial bias.

title: State v. Vega-Larregui
description: Whether the temporary authorization of virtual grand jury presentations during a public health emergency violates the constitutional right to a grand jury indictment.
plaintiff_argument: The virtual grand jury format is a necessary and constitutional temporary measure during the pandemic, with safeguards ensuring fairness and integrity, allowing the justice system to continue.
defendant_argument: The virtual grand jury format violates constitutional rights, including the right to a grand jury presentation, secrecy, a fair cross-section of the community, and equal protection, and the Court lacked authority to implement it.
decision_outcome: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss the indictment, ruling that virtual grand jury proceedings during the pandemic do not violate constitutional rights.

title: State v. Lopez-Carrera
description: Whether the Criminal Justice Reform Act (CJRA) empowers judges to detain non-citizen defendants to prevent immigration officials from removing them from the country before trial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the CJRA does not impose a volitional act requirement for detention and that pretrial detention is warranted when a defendant's deportation is certain and imminent to assure their appearance in court.
defendant_argument: The defendants contend that the CJRA's risk of non-appearance only applies to a defendant's voluntary acts, not to actions by third parties like ICE, and therefore does not authorize detention based on the risk of deportation.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Appellate Division's judgment, ruling that the CJRA does not authorize judges to detain non-citizen defendants solely to prevent their removal by ICE.

title: Rozenblit v. Lyles
description: Whether the provisions in a collective negotiations agreement (CNA) allowing for "release time" for public school employees are statutorily authorized and do not violate the Gift Clause of the New Jersey Constitution, as argued by the defendant, or if they are unauthorized and constitute an unconstitutional gift of public funds, as argued by the plaintiffs.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the District's payment of salaries and benefits for employees on "release time" violates the New Jersey Constitution's Gift Clause because it serves private purposes, not public welfare, and is not statutorily authorized.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the release time provisions are statutorily authorized under N.J.S.A. 18A:30-7 and other Education Code provisions, and do not violate the Gift Clause as they serve a public purpose by promoting labor peace and efficient collective bargaining.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Appellate Division's judgment and reinstated the trial court's order dismissing the plaintiffs' claims, thereby upholding the legality of the release time provisions.
